competencies.justification: Understanding India's integrated contribution to Social Science is the chapter's organising purpose. The opening definitional passage frames Social Science as the systematic, interconnected study of human society; 'Social Science as a Study of Disciplines' establishes that no single field can explain society; and the four discipline sections plus the closing 'Secondary-Stage Social Science' synthesis present them 'together presenting a comprehensive understanding of the world.' India's own contributions are woven in throughout — the Pañchamahābhūtas and vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam, the Arthaśhāstra, the itihāsa-purāṇa tradition, dharma/artha/rājadharma, Panchayati Raj, and India's economic history. The chapter would have no purpose without it; the title and the concluding synthesis both name this idea.

The 'History' section is a dedicated, self-contained section that develops understanding of explaining the past using different types of sources with specific examples from Indian history. It sets out literary and archaeological sources and then presents, with captioned Indian examples, the four source families — literary (the Sāmaveda manuscript, a palm-leaf Tirukkuṟaḷ), archaeological (a Sindhu-Sarasvatī terracotta figurine, a Viṣhṇu sculpture), epigraphic (a Gupta-period Brahmi inscription, Krishnadeva Raya's Kannada inscription at Hampi), and numismatic (a Samudragupta coin, a Mughal coin of Jahangir) — alongside modern methods such as carbon-14 dating and archaeology. This section could be taught as a lesson in its own right on how historians use sources.

'Understanding Society through Time and Traditions' is a dedicated, self-contained section that develops the growth of new indigenous ideas across India in Philosophy and Social Science — precisely the demand this C-code names. It presents the Pañchamahābhūtas as an early philosophical model of nature as an interconnected system, vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam as an idea of human interdependence, and the Arthaśhāstra attributed to Kauṭilya (composed about 2,300 years ago) as systematic thinking on administration, taxation, and the duties of rulers, arguing that such indigenous inquiry into society long predates modern academic disciplines. This section could be taught as a lesson in its own right on India's intellectual traditions.

The 'Geography' section is a dedicated, self-contained section developing the inter-relationship between human beings and their physical environment. It defines Geography as the study of the relationships between human societies and their surroundings, examining how people interact with the natural environment and how places influence human life — for instance, how India's long coastline shaped its global interactions. The section introduces the discipline's tools (maps, globes, atlases, GIS, infographics), and its LET'S EXPLORE box has students map their own village or city on NCERT's School Bhuvan portal. This section could be taught as a lesson in its own right; the chapter's central focus lies elsewhere.

The 'Political Science' section is a dedicated, self-contained section that develops understanding of governance and the features and history of democratic government in India. It defines Political Science as the study of how power is distributed, decisions are made, and policies implemented across constitutions, governments, and State institutions, and uses India's Panchayati Raj system as an embodiment of grassroots democracy and local self-governance; it traces India's early political thought (dharma, artha, rājadharma, the Arthaśhāstra) and links these ideas to modern democratic practice. This section could be taught as a lesson in its own right on governance and democracy; the chapter's central focus lies elsewhere.

The 'Economics' section is a dedicated, self-contained section that develops understanding of the key features of the economy that this C-code enumerates — production, distribution, and exchange. It defines Economics as the study of how limited resources are used to meet needs, how goods and services are produced, exchanged, and distributed, and how consumers, producers, and governments make decisions balancing goals such as growth and stability or efficiency and fairness, and it situates these features in India's economic history from a leading pre-colonial trading economy to post-independence development. This section could be taught as a lesson in its own right on how an economy works; the chapter's central focus lies elsewhere.
